content: This is the discussion thread for #General announcements > Association for Human Mathematics.
I empathize, but without reevaluation of values this won't fly. I have my ideas for programming, but they are not ready yet.

Anatole Dedecker said:

I believe that members of our community have a significant role to play in this endeavour, as we have been exposed somewhat earlier to the destructive behaviour of AI companies, and because Lean and Mathlib have unfortunatly become key infrastructure in these developments.

I object this framing, seeing it as pretty unfair to the AI companies. For at least a year, we were telling the AI companies "Do not publish just PDF's with the results, no one is going to check them, and they are likely wrong anyway. Formalize it first, and then we can talk." And when they finally do what they are asked for, and publish every math result with a formalization, we accuse them of "abusing" Lean & Mathlib?
I would like to join, but rule 1 on membership prevents me to do so due to my work on formal-conjectures on behalf of GDM...
I don’t see why we have any obligation to be “fair” to AI companies. If they want to participate in mathematical activity, they need to conform to human math academic norms.

My stance is slightly different from the association. I believe human mathematicians can put AI to legitimate uses. The current ownership of AI models and the incentives of its owners presents a fundamental obstacle to ensuring such legitimate use is protected. But mathematics is fundamentally a human endeavour to understand patterns through abstractions. It is for mathematicians to set norms. AI companies sell useful tools. They are not stakeholders.

@Anatole Dedecker thanks for the link! Can you clarify two things? Does 1 mean that one doesn't actively collaborate with them or that one doesn't provide any mathematical insight (for example asking a question)? In 2, do you know how code or a picture are treated?

Shreyas Srinivas said:

I don’t see why we have any obligation to be “fair” to AI companies. If they want to participate in mathematical activity, they need to conform to human math academic norms.

An important note here is: if X and Y have hitherto always gone together, and a norm is expressed as "do X", and then AI finds a way to do X without Y and we say "no, we meant Y", that isn't unfair or changing the rules after the event, it simply illustrates how such statements can't be expected to distinguish meaningfully between things that have never been meaningfully different before. Indeed, much of the insight gained from AI has been about making such distinctions (and showing how asking about AGI was asking the wrong question, because there are so many different forms of intelligence, and AI has progressed in different areas at different rates).

Of course norms can also change over time in response to outside factors; mathematics isn't simply a game that can be won by following a set of rules fixed at some time in the past.

I am not going to join this association, and I advise readers of this thread to not join.

This is because the very idea of "human mathematics" is philosophically absurd.

At its core, mathematics is the pursuit of truth in some parts of the world, like all the other sciences (physics, chemistry, economics, etc.) Truth is by definition independent of whatever discovered it. If we discount LLM-generated mathematics as truth, we are not doing the best we can do. It is like dismissing Nemo's "The Code" simply because they are nonbinary.

Put another way, the viewpoint of the association seems to be that LLM-generated mathematics is Bokmål and that it should be completely replaced by Nynorsk (human mathematics). Neither side is better than the other in expressing truth, and indeed the sum may be strictly greater than its parts.
This is not just about philosophy.
I know – but I fear, I actually fear, that the association will cause a schism in the mathematical community.
Suppose that AI solves, say, BSD and you work in this area. It's unlikely that your can ignore it and promise your future research will never cite that

Jeremy Tan said:

I know – but I fear, I actually fear, that the association will cause a schism in the mathematical community.

It is not clear to me that people refusing to use AI would be more responsible for a schism than people accepting to use AI.

Jeremy Tan said:

At its core, mathematics is the pursuit of truth in some parts of the world

I think many philosophers of mathematicians would disagree with your statement here. In particular, I can easily write a little program that outputs as many true sentences about natural numbers as you like: its output goes "1 = 1", "2 = 2", "3 = 3", "4 = 4", and so on until we run out of patience. Even though this program creates a lot of truth very quickly, intuitively I would not say it is good at maths.

I claim that therefore deciding which truths are worthwile is an essential part of maths. And I have not been convinced thus far that anything output by a language model has been worth my while.

Although I would still actively engage in LLM usage, I share the views and sentiments behind these 3 rules listed in Membership commitment.

Besides the obvious ideas, rule 1 is also about not to actively feed the proprietary model training process with "de-identified data" thus supporting AI companies to overclaim and benefit from it and keep disrupting the value of all human professions, rule 2 is also about preventing such generated texts polluting our intellectual fruit and the quality bar associated with them, and rule 3 is also about protecting our thinking process from the pollution of generated texts, which may make us lazier (outsourcing our thinking, or no longer working on open problems "solved" by AI and settle on "digesting"), addictive (no longer persistent to go through the hardship and long lone journeys), or losing the ability to recognize the quality of a work (correctness, depth, taste etc.).

They are most devastating to the education for generations to come. Before "AI" era, I was never able to imagine that humanity could lose touch with intelligence beyond using them like a blackbox, and now I can. I consider this as an extinction level event and one of the great filters for us. The rare talented mathematicians (or domain experts in general) that can lead a civilization leap through such barriers are already barely nurtured and cherished by our civilization, and their survival through the "the Great Ravine" of human intelligence and values is not guaranteed, and their extinction leads to the extinction for the rest of us, in face of so many great challenges ahead.

People with faith in SGI or RSI or whatever the term they use for such a creature, knowing that the model training still need to feed on great minds than standing on their own feet, still recklessly cause the disruptions that we have all witnessed recently, and there would be no end and no limit despite some of them may disagree or quit or change their view or actions. That is one prominent side of historical trend, and there are diverse sides that we can join to unite to prevent it from devouring all of us. Strict rules to join AHM is imperfect but reasonable and even crucial for one of such sides or forces.

That said (and I apologize in advance if my opinions hurt anyone's feelings, and admins please feel free to delete or edit this post, but this is likely the only post I would express such strong opinion on this Zulip, and I really can't predict the ramifications of this post), my actions might still be actively violating these 3 rules as written, for the spirit behind these 3 rules, because "there is only one way to find out (by doing it)". The important thing here is to use new technologies responsibly, with clear boundary and proactively evolving ethics (but not excuses like we have seen in recent events), and most of all, with our own intelligence. That said again, I stand by 138 (and counting) members that have joined the association, and best wishes for a bright future of AHM.

Footnote: It may be a tipping point that great minds once embrace the use of new technologies may start to shift focus to preserve something more traditional, e.g. as in one of Tao's comments, "I do not regret my past efforts to raise awareness of the potential of AI in mathematics......But in the immediate term, the most pressing issue is for the entire mathematical community to unite around our core values and objectives".

Jeremy Tan said:

At its core, mathematics is the pursuit of truth in some parts of the world, like all the other sciences (physics, chemistry, economics, etc.) Truth is by definition independent of whatever discovered it. If we discount LLM-generated mathematics as truth, we are not doing the best we can do. It is like dismissing Nemo's "The Code" simply because they are nonbinary.

This assumes proof-irrelevance.

In other words, that content of a proof does not matter, the only thing that matter is it's existence. Assuming this, human mathematics indeed cannot be defended.

As I said, this kind of initiatives can't work without reevaluation of values.

This sort of thing has however been around as a theme in science fiction for a very long time, e.g. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Feeling_of_Power

(And there is a well-known trend in parts of the tech industry of trying to implement ideas they got from science fiction, without regard to whether that science fiction was in fact cautioning against those ideas.)
If you have not read "The Evolution of Human Science", a short story by Ted Chiang, this thread seems like an opportune moment to insist that you read it.

Joseph Myers said:

This sort of thing has however been around as a theme in science fiction for a very long time, e.g. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Feeling_of_Power

I got the ideas of technological deskilling from science fictions since I was a child, as well as the ideas of robots that deem humans as unnecessary or obstacles. I just was unable to imagine them actually happening in reality as in how.

But living in a time that commercial AI companies actively disrupt the values of human professions and subtly undermine human intelligence to promote the intelligence of their models (e.g. not citing the major authors developed the theory and framework in the first revision of writeup, being implicitly proud that they don't have a research level subject expert after getting an answer for open problems by automated research, or actively denying their existence in the team or the use of heavy human steering during generation, or listing subject experts as secondary authors while crediting them only by their digestion work, or more commonly only in acknowledgement for reviewing the math while holding their career as endorsement), and young students actively consider humans as the negative factor in agent-assisted research compared to relinquishing to automated research, now I can.

Years ago when I started to learn more about Lean 3, I imagined that AI development would enable developing domain specific tactics or theoretical frameworks. But in reality frontier models rush to a pile of certificates by using Lean like an assembly language, instead of developing intermediate techniques like domain specific tactics and proper math APIs (they don't even emit Lean in a well organized manner, leaving the community to purchase much more tokens to digest them than they were first generated by entities in possession of enormous compute). Same attitude is applied to automated math research that these models don't develop theories and understanding but rush to seemingly solving the open problems. That is also what I could not have imagined, a low-quality brutal-force intelligence that happens to work for earlier open problems (standing on the shoulders of human developed theories and techniques), combining with humans undermining their own intelligence. Imagine that dark future facing challenges ahead, now I can.

(To be clear, I am not saying that these technologies are not good by nitpicking on current defects, they are amazing work by human intelligence, I am simply criticizing overclaiming and describing how that may distort the perceptions of the public and students, and have ramifications for our future. And that is one of the reasons why AHM rules are reasonable, while seemingly too conservative. Is it already the time we have lost the imagination of preparing students for doing the hard portion of research by pen-and-paper?)

Kim Morrison said:

If you have not read "The Evolution of Human Science", a short story by Ted Chiang, this thread seems like an opportune moment to insist that you read it.

Except it's blocked by a paywall....

From https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Evolution_of_Human_Science :

The development of the metahumans' science becomes so advanced that it forces the ordinary scientists to switch to interpreting and decoding the metahumans' achievements, because common people are no longer able to create anything fundamentally new. The science then becomes the means of seeking and establishing communication with the super-intelligent metahumans.

That is exactly the opposite to the reality that the frontier models are "not creating anything fundamentally new" (yet), while it can be observed at least on arxiv that human mathematicians are proving classical theorems using new methods with conceptual advances in recent months, those methods would lead to a wave of new results to be proven by merely "AI". So instead of downplaying the roles of humans to digesting the "AI" results, we should realize that it's the models that are digesting our intellectual fruits.

Existing claims scooped by frontier models, merely suggest that our civilization is not funding pure mathematicians sufficiently to pursue those problems with deep understanding and without concerns of livelihood or career, leaving them open for decades (actually progressing in a pace and on verge of a breakthrough, and the other side of story is that some other interesting problems were being worked on too). Instead, our civilization chose to pour capitals into an inefficient model architecture, believing in rounds of new scaling laws, and letting the hype to jeopardize our future (e.g. environment, young talents, an open research atmosphere etc.).

As individuals, the least we can do is not to buy in any stories indicating human researchers are obsolete or already reliant on "AI", and stay focus on the research journey, and use all available techniques and our minds to their full potential, instead of fully surrendering to one of such techniques that has "neural", "intelligence" in its branding while being neither (it is a data/compute-eager statistical method with great success, but far from neuroscience research, and a different mechanism from human intelligence).

Riccardo Brasca said:

Anatole Dedecker thanks for the link! Can you clarify two things? Does 1 mean that one doesn't actively collaborate with them or that one doesn't provide any mathematical insight (for example asking a question)? In 2, do you know how code or a picture are treated?

These are good questions, which I believe do not have official answers yet. I will answer with my vision of things (not representative of the association in any way).

For your first question, I think it depends on the situation. I believe rule 1 should prohibit any form of interaction with a draft before it is publically released; in particular, if members receive things like "hey, we proved this fancy thing, could you tell us what you think before we release it" from an AI company, I would expect them to refuse. What happens after the draft is public is more subtle of course, and then it depends a lot on what your question is and what the context is.

For the second question, I interpret the rule as "I will not expose people reading my work to any form of output of a LLM". So I think members should not include any AI-generated pictures in their work, nor should they include AI-generated code as part of the published material. In particular, my view of things is that rule 2 bans publishing, or contributing to Mathlib, any AI-generated formalization, because a formalization is a mathematical text. However, I think rule 2 would allow, for example, getting AI-help to write some invisible bits of LaTeX, or to write a TikZ figure, or to write a Python script to plot some data. Another example is that rule 2 says it is completly fine to use the new slopified (:sob:) version of Detexify.

Wikipedia says:

Since 2025, it has integrated extensive generative AI tools, including options to generate essays from scratch, to suggest and insert citations, to "humanize" the text to avoid it being flagged as AI-generated, and to predict grades based on user input on the instructor, course, and university.

So I think so, yes. But this is my opinion.

I don’t see why we have any obligation to be “fair” to AI companies. If they want to participate in mathematical activity, they need to conform to human math academic norms.

Why, exactly?  Math doesn't belong to the academy.  I get to find out things about the world and share what I find with others without asking anyone's permission.

Now maybe you just define 'participate in mathematical activity' as participating in current institutions and practices, rather than what I'd call, well, doing math. If all you're saying is "look, if you want to hang with the popular kids you have to follow our rules; here's your cap, wear it backwards, or put a sticker on it for some reason", okay, sure, that's your call. Groups can define their own rules and gatekeep entry, for reasons both good and bad. But that's a peer-pressure appeal which only works on people who care about being in the clique in the first place.

Now some of the math academic community's current norms make sense to me, and if I break them I can see how that would be, at best, sub-optimal.  Others seem very self-destructive. None seem binding on outsiders.

TBH recent discussions have sounded a lot like FIDE trying to say they're the only ones who can call something a world championship of chess, because they've elected themselves to the position of somehow owning rights to a game they didn't invent.  This seems only natural to the insiders -- good for us = good -- and to be fair it's not always, or even mostly, pure self-interest talking, but from the outside it doesn't seem very persuasive.

What's clear is that "you have no power over me", as she said to the Goblin King.

I have several questions about Rule 3 of AHM. The rule states that “members of the AI-free caucus do not use AI models in a research capacity.” Does this mean that:

  1. members cannot use AI to learn an area that they are not familiar with?

  2. members cannot use AI to summarize existing literature or help search for relevant papers? members cannot use tools like https://leansearch.net/, https://leandex.projectnumina.ai/, or maybe just ask an LLM to find or search for relevant theorems in Mathlib?

  3. members cannot use AI to translate mathematical papers written in languages that they are not fluent with?

  4. members cannot cite or make use of research papers that were produced with the assistance of AI, even if the results are state of the art, formally verified in Lean, accepted by a well-known journal, or independently peer-reviewed by other mathematicians?

I want to emphasize that I am not asking these questions in order to be hostile. I am genuinely curious about where the boundary of “using AI models in a research capacity” is intended to lie, and about the caucus’s position on cases such as these.

I feel like... AI mathematics is human mathematics. It's humans building these tools. The people at OpenAI and Anthropic, yes, but not just them. Lean and mathlib in particular have been a great help to AI in math. All of these tools trained on Lean and mathlib to learn mathematics and formalization and everyone who has contributed to Lean or mathlib should be proud of playing a part in helping make this possible. Even everyone who has published a paper, you helped build the training data. You deserve credit, and when AI in math has a victory, you should feel like it's a little bit your victory too.

What's clear is that "you have no power over me", as she said to the Goblin King.

Math has had this division of academy and outsiders long before LLMs. Some of those outsiders have, within academic norms, contributed substantially to mathematics. There have also been others who have chosen to ignore these norms who have “contributed” in their own way. Academy endured all this and managed to retain its rules and its position of respect and prestige. Nobody is forced to follow these rules and be a part of academia. But academia is not obliged to accommodate people who do not wish to abide by them either.

"and its position of respect and prestige" <- I appreciate your honesty there, as I think this is actually an important and under-addressed motivation, the concern about preserving a kind of elevated social status, at least in your own circles.

It can definitely be jarring when a skill that's rare, requires years of difficult practice and training to master, requires considerable sacrifices of lifestyle, and doesn't always get rewarded in other ways (such as pay), becomes one of only several ways to achieve an end. The peasants flood in chaotically, and not always with the highest quality products at first. It can feel like some of the toolset you've developed isn't as important as it was, and if that's something you really care about and see as part of your identity, it can be very disorienting. We've seen this happen in many other fields over the centuries with the same response from extant guilds. AI is qualitatively different in its scope, but people themselves haven't changed much.

For privately funded components of the math community, I say let all the flowers bloom and we'll see what happens. For publicly funded groups the question is a little more complicated, but even there I think a diversity of approaches is best to start with, and that seems to be what we're likely to get. So if some AHM member refuses to look at a theorem because the author used GenAI to find the proof, I'm going to roll my eyes but there's no point getting annoyed by it. As I said, you can set your own standards; other people will simply develop competing ones, and I expect those will succeed, but if I were better at predicting things I'd be reading in the shade on a beach by now.

From my perspective, what's happened is that math proofs have now entered the realm of experiments that most people can perform, experiments which it's possible to guarantee were correctly performed. Those explorations are data which we'll have to make sense of and put in its proper place, deciding what's important and what's not, and figuring out the right perspectives and connections.

IOW: welcome to physics. Come on in, the water's fine. :sunglasses:

I got an answer to a research question (a citation to a existing theorem I just couldn't find any record of in the literature) accidentally from a google search's auto-generated AI answer. I couldn't unsee the reference to that paper, and to do due diligence I couldn't ignore the suggestion. I also had an argument suggested by a colleague, but my gut was telling me that surely this was a known thing. Do I have to confess to relying on a automatic AI service in my paper to get a citation and so disqualify myself from AHM?

Douglas McNeil said:

The peasants flood in chaotically, and not always with the highest quality products at first.

I think you severely misunderstand the point and are deliberately looking for a gotcha here... which this ain't. Mathematics is and will always be about humans understanding patterns with abstractions and training themselves to think, communicate, and pass on this knowledge better. We don't exclude anybody from participating because of some aristocratic prestige but because they haven't put in the work to understand and eventually synthesize mathematics, trace and attribute ideas properly, and teach it further. AI is not going to suddenly give anyone a pass from doing this hard work.

It's also a bit rich to call trillion dollar AI companies and their acolytes "peasants" when they are the ones trying to bypass said hard work, using models trained on stolen information, using work without citation, and trying to jump into a bandwagon nobody asked them to, and acting entitled to treat the community with disrespect for its norms. Sounds all very aristocratic to me.

I am really sad to see this hatred towards an emergent technology, and how much positive feedback such posts are getting.
Some concerns about AI are valid, some uses of AI irresponsible.
I am not at all against people doing research / programming without any AI help -- there is a value & beauty to it similarly as there is a value & beauty of going for a hike as opposed to a road-trip.

However, I would not want to go for a hike with a group of people who sound as if they wished all the cars to blow up. That is my main reason why I would not want to join, and advise others not to.

These examples are getting hilariously strawman-like.

My two cents: @Anatole Dedecker 's view is a stronger version of rule 2. Rule 2 as written is about articulating the mathematical ideas by human authorship.

Carefully crafted formalizations like PRs to Mathlib are theory building and idea resonation across mathematical branches/areas, they are a form of mathematical text. Members committing to the spirit of rule 2 will treat it as such.

If a newcomer used AI as a baby walker, and familiarized themselves with how something can be expressed in Lean to the point that they are already able to write the same Lean code themselves as mathematical ideas modulo some Lean technicality, it is like checking with a dictionary or literatures or manuals. In spirit this shouldn't count as "starting with a base of AI activity". Only the LLM users still heavily rely on rounds of prompting or pure LLM autoformalization without inspecting, tweaking and digesting the code, then PR them to Mathlib etc., should be explicitly considered a violation of rule 2. An exception is that, similar to examples in Anatole's message, using AI to set up Lean and Mathlib environment, or handle chores such as bumping versions, environment debugging etc. should not be considered as a violation of rule 2.

Publishing AI-generated formalization, in a broader sense, such as sharing it in a public repository or contributing to Tau Ceti (I know Anatole would disagree to this), should not directly qualify as communicating mathematical idea, thus are not violating rule 2. In a stricter sense, if such AI generated formalization is the main mathematical content to be published to Arxiv or journals that allows such a submission, should be considered as a violation of rule 2. An exception may be a human authored mathematical text but verfied by AI generated formalization concurrently (which seems to fall into the jurisdiction of rule 3, or even fall through it).

I think the rules are not written with formalization in mind. In the more traditional practice of mathematics, I think the distinction between rule 2 and rule 3 is pretty clear: if you are not in the AI-free caucus, you are free to chat with an LLM to get ideas and proofs, but then you have to fully write the paper yourself. Formalization is slightly more subtle because it is harder to disentangle the "ideas" from the "mathematical text".
